Multigrid is one of the great algorithms for numerically solving PDEs; it is
one of the few essentially optimal algorithms for solving a linear system of
equations, since it computes the solution of an $N\times N$ system in
$\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$ -- or even just $\mathcal{O}(N)$ -- operations.

This page is meant to accompany a reading of
[Section 4.6 of Randall LeVeque's text on finite difference methods](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717839.ch4).
Other good resources are cited there.  It is an HTML version of a
[Jupyter notebook](https://github.com/ketch/AMCS-252-2026/blob/main/in-class%20notebook/Multigrid.ipynb)
from my course on finite difference methods (AMCS 252).  The notebook
includes a Python implementation of everything shown here, which you can run
and modify; some of that code is reproduced below in collapsible boxes.  On
this page, the computations run in your browser.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Functions shared by the interactive figures below.  They are JavaScript
// ports of the Python functions in the notebook.
lib = {
  const phi = x => 20 * Math.PI * x ** 3;
  // Right-hand side f(x) = u''(x) for the exact solution below.
  const f = x => -20 + 0.5 * 120 * Math.PI * x * Math.cos(phi(x))
                 - 0.5 * (60 * Math.PI * x ** 2) ** 2 * Math.sin(phi(x));
  const uExact = x => 1 + 12 * x - 10 * x ** 2 + 0.5 * Math.sin(phi(x));
  const alpha = 1, beta = 3;

  // Interior grid points of a grid with m interior points.
  const grid = m => Float64Array.from({length: m}, (_, i) => (i + 1) / (m + 1));
  // Straight line from alpha to beta at m points (the initial guess).
  const line = m => Float64Array.from({length: m}, (_, i) => alpha + (beta - alpha) * i / (m - 1));

  // Restriction: keep the odd-numbered points.
  const coarsen = v => v.filter((_, i) => i % 2 === 1);

  // Prolongation: linear interpolation from m points to 2m+1 points,
  // with boundary values a and b.
  function interpolate(v, a, b) {
    const mc = v.length, out = new Float64Array(2 * mc + 1);
    for (let i = 0; i < mc; i++) out[2 * i + 1] = v[i];
    for (let i = 0; i < mc - 1; i++) out[2 * i + 2] = 0.5 * (v[i] + v[i + 1]);
    out[0] = 0.5 * (out[1] + a);
    out[2 * mc] = 0.5 * (out[2 * mc - 1] + b);
    return out;
  }

  // One damped Jacobi step for U'' = rhs with U(0) = a, U(1) = b.
  function jacobiStep(U, rhs, a, b, w) {
    const m = U.length, h = 1 / (m + 1), V = new Float64Array(m);
    for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {
      const left = i > 0 ? U[i - 1] : a;
      const right = i < m - 1 ? U[i + 1] : b;
      V[i] = (1 - w) * U[i] + w * (0.5 * (left + right) - 0.5 * h * h * rhs[i]);
    }
    return V;
  }

  // Residual rhs - AU, where A is the second-difference matrix.
  function residual(U, rhs, a, b) {
    const m = U.length, h = 1 / (m + 1), r = new Float64Array(m);
    for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {
      const left = i > 0 ? U[i - 1] : a;
      const right = i < m - 1 ? U[i + 1] : b;
      r[i] = rhs[i] - (left - 2 * U[i] + right) / (h * h);
    }
    return r;
  }

  // nu damped Jacobi steps (omega = 2/3, as in the notebook's Jacobi function).
  // Returns the new iterate and its residual.
  function jacobi(U, rhs, a, b, nu, w = 2 / 3) {
    for (let s = 0; s < nu; s++) U = jacobiStep(U, rhs, a, b, w);
    return [U, residual(U, rhs, a, b)];
  }

  // Exact solution of the discrete system AU = F (Thomas algorithm).
  function solveDiscrete(F, a, b) {
    const n = F.length, h = 1 / (n + 1);
    const d = Float64Array.from(F, v => v * h * h);
    d[0] -= a; d[n - 1] -= b;
    const c = new Float64Array(n), g = new Float64Array(n);
    c[0] = -0.5; g[0] = -0.5 * d[0];
    for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
      const den = -2 - c[i - 1];
      c[i] = 1 / den;
      g[i] = (d[i] - g[i - 1]) / den;
    }
    const U = new Float64Array(n);
    U[n - 1] = g[n - 1];
    for (let i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) U[i] = g[i] - c[i] * U[i + 1];
    return U;
  }

  const maxAbs = a => a.reduce((s, v) => Math.max(s, Math.abs(v)), 0);
  const linspace = (a, b, n) => Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => a + (b - a) * i / (n - 1));

  return {phi, f, uExact, alpha, beta, grid, line, coarsen, interpolate,
          jacobiStep, residual, jacobi, solveDiscrete, maxAbs, linspace};
}
```

## Jacobi's method

We use Jacobi's method to solve the problem given by Eq. (4.82) in the text:

$$
u''(x) = f(x), \qquad 0 < x < 1, \qquad u(0) = \alpha = 1, \quad u(1) = \beta = 3,
$$

where $f$ is chosen so that the exact solution is

$$
u(x) = 1 + 12x - 10x^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(20\pi x^3).
$$

We use a grid with $m = 2^8 - 1 = 255$ interior points $x_i = ih$ and mesh
width $h = 1/(m+1)$.  The approximation $U_i \approx u(x_i)$ satisfies the
centered difference equations

$$
\frac{U_{i-1} - 2U_i + U_{i+1}}{h^2} = f(x_i), \qquad i = 1, \dots, m,
$$

with $U_0 = \alpha$ and $U_{m+1} = \beta$.  We write this linear system as
$AU = F$, where the boundary values have been moved into the first and last
entries of $F$.  Here is the exact solution:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: "u(x)", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.line(lib.linspace(0, 1, 1000), {x: d => d, y: lib.uExact, strokeWidth: 2})]
})
```

The (under-relaxed) Jacobi iteration with parameter $\omega$ is

$$
U_i \leftarrow (1-\omega)\, U_i + \omega \left( \frac{U_{i-1} + U_{i+1}}{2} - \frac{h^2}{2} f(x_i) \right).
$$

With $\omega = 1$ this is the original Jacobi method.  Below, we start from
a straight line from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ as the initial guess and take up to
100 iterations.  The slider sets the number of iterations shown.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof jacIter = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "Iterations"})
viewof jacOmega = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: tex`\omega`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
jacobiRun = {
  const m = 2 ** 8 - 1, x = lib.grid(m), F = x.map(lib.f);
  let U = lib.line(m);
  const iterates = [U];
  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    U = lib.jacobiStep(U, F, lib.alpha, lib.beta, jacOmega);
    iterates.push(U);
  }
  return {x, u: x.map(lib.uExact), iterates};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const U = jacobiRun.iterates[jacIter];
  const pts = Array.from(jacobiRun.x, (x, i) => ({x, U: U[i], err: U[i] - jacobiRun.u[i]}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 420,
    title: `Number of iterations: ${jacIter}`,
    x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
    y: {label: null, domain: [-3, 6], grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Exact", "Jacobi", "Error"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.line(lib.linspace(0, 1, 1000), {x: d => d, y: lib.uExact, stroke: () => "Exact", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "U", stroke: () => "Jacobi", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "err", stroke: () => "Error", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}
```

Move the slider and notice how the high-frequency components of the error are
damped very quickly, but the low-frequency error barely changes.  This is
because the matrix appearing in Jacobi's method is tridiagonal, so in a single
iteration each solution point only "feels" the values of its immediate
neighbors.  It takes very many iterations for low-frequency information to
propagate.  As we'll see, part of the power of multigrid lies in enabling
information to propagate rapidly between distant points in the solution.

### Under-relaxation

Try changing the number of Jacobi iterations and $\omega$ above, and see how
the error changes.  Remember that the $p$th Fourier mode

$$
u^p_j = \sin(p\pi x_j)
$$

is multiplied in each iteration by the factor $\hat{\gamma}_p$, where

$$
|\hat{\gamma}_p| = |1-\omega + \omega\cos(p\pi h)| = |1 + \omega(\cos(p \pi h) - 1)|.
$$

The plot below shows these values for a grid with $m = 30$ interior points.
The modes in the second half ($p \ge (m+1)/2$, where
$-1 < \cos(p\pi h) \le 0$) are the high-frequency modes that Jacobi's method
should damp.  For these modes, $\hat{\gamma}_p$ lies between $1-2\omega$ and
$1-\omega$, so

$$
\max_{p \ge (m+1)/2} |\hat{\gamma}_p| \le \max\left(|1-\omega|,\, |1-2\omega|\right).
$$

The right-hand side is smallest when $1-\omega = 2\omega-1$, that is, for
$\omega = 2/3$, where it equals $1/3$.  This is the reason for choosing
$\omega = 2/3$: every high-frequency mode is reduced by at least a factor of 3
in each iteration.  Try $\omega = 2/3$ in the plot.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof dampOmega = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: tex`\omega`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const M = 30, H = 1 / (M + 1);
  const pts = Array.from({length: M}, (_, i) => {
    const p = i + 1;
    return {p, g: Math.abs(1 + dampOmega * (Math.cos(p * Math.PI * H) - 1))};
  });
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 380,
    title: `ω = ${dampOmega.toFixed(2)}`,
    x: {label: "p", domain: [0, M]},
    y: {label: "|γ̂ₚ|", domain: [0, 1], grid: true},
    marks: [Plot.dot(pts, {x: "p", y: "g", fill: "currentColor", r: 4})]
  });
}
```

Notice that for $\omega=1$ the highest frequencies are also not damped much.

### Grid representations of a given frequency

The plot below shows the mode $\sin(p\pi x)$ (thin line) and its values on a
grid with $m$ interior points (dots).  Notice how a *low-frequency* mode
(one with many points per wavelength) on a fine grid becomes a
*high-frequency* mode (one with very few points per wavelength) on a coarser
grid.  Eventually, on grids with very few points, the mode is *aliased* to a
completely different mode.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sineM = Inputs.range([1, 63], {value: 15, step: 1, label: "m (interior points)"})
viewof sineP = Inputs.range([0, 50], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "p (frequency)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const xs = lib.linspace(0, 1, sineM + 2);
  const pts = xs.map(x => ({x, y: Math.sin(sineP * Math.PI * x)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 380,
    title: `sin(${sineP}πx) with m = ${sineM} points`,
    x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
    y: {label: null, domain: [-1.2, 1.2], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(lib.linspace(0, 1, 1000), {x: d => d, y: d => Math.sin(sineP * Math.PI * d),
                                            stroke: "red", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "y", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(pts, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "currentColor", r: 4})
    ]
  });
}
```

## Restriction and prolongation

The multigrid idea is to solve successively on different grids, so that every
mode has a small damping factor $\hat{\gamma}$ on some grid.

To implement multigrid, we need a way to take a function with values on a fine
grid and restrict it to its values on a coarser grid (*restriction*).  We also
need a way to take a function with values on a coarse grid and interpolate
onto a fine grid (*prolongation*).  Here we use the simplest choices.  If the
fine grid has $m = 2m_c + 1$ interior points, the coarse grid has $m_c$
interior points, located at the fine-grid points
$x_2, x_4, \dots, x_{2m_c}$.  (The comments in the Python code below call
these the odd-numbered points, because Python numbers them from 0.)

- Restriction keeps the values at those points and discards the others.
- Prolongation copies the coarse-grid values to those points and sets each
  remaining fine-grid value to the average of its two neighbors (linear
  interpolation), using the boundary values at the ends.

<details>
<summary>Python code from the notebook</summary>

```python
def coarsen(f):
    return f[1::2]  # This slicing just takes the odd-numbered points

def interpolate(f,alpha,beta):
    m_coarse=len(f)
    m_fine  =2*m_coarse+1
    f_interp = np.zeros(m_fine)
    f_interp[1::2]=f                       #Set the values of the odd numbered points
    f_interp[2:-1:2]=0.5*(f[:-1]+f[1:])    #Set the values of the (interior) even numbered points
    f_interp[0]=0.5*(f_interp[1]+alpha)    #Set the values of the endpoints
    f_interp[-1]=0.5*(f_interp[-2]+beta)
    return f_interp
```

</details>

## Correction using a second grid

Now we take the result $U$ of 100 iterations of the original Jacobi method
($\omega = 1$) from above, compute the residual

$$
r = F - AU
$$

on the fine grid.  If $U^*$ denotes the exact solution of $AU = F$, then the
error $e = U - U^*$ satisfies

$$
Ae = -r.
$$

We restrict $r$ to the coarse grid and approximately solve this equation
there (with $A$ replaced by the corresponding coarse-grid matrix), using
3 iterations of under-relaxed
Jacobi with $\omega = 2/3$, starting from $e = 0$.  Then we interpolate $e$
to the fine grid and subtract it from the fine-grid solution.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
twoGrid = {
  const m = 2 ** 8 - 1, x = lib.grid(m), F = x.map(lib.f), u = x.map(lib.uExact);
  let U = lib.line(m);
  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) U = lib.jacobiStep(U, F, lib.alpha, lib.beta, 1);
  const r = lib.residual(U, F, lib.alpha, lib.beta);
  const r2 = lib.coarsen(r);
  let e2 = new Float64Array(r2.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) e2 = lib.jacobiStep(e2, r2.map(v => -v), 0, 0, 2 / 3);
  const e = lib.interpolate(e2, 0, 0);
  const Unew = U.map((v, j) => v - e[j]);
  return {
    pts: Array.from(x, (xi, i) => ({x: xi, u: u[i], U: Unew[i], err: Unew[i] - u[i]})),
    errBefore: lib.maxAbs(U.map((v, i) => v - u[i])),
    errAfter: lib.maxAbs(Unew.map((v, i) => v - u[i]))
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 420,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: null, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Exact", "Corrected", "Error"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0]),
    Plot.line(twoGrid.pts, {x: "x", y: "u", stroke: () => "Exact", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(twoGrid.pts, {x: "x", y: "U", stroke: () => "Corrected", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(twoGrid.pts, {x: "x", y: "err", stroke: () => "Error", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Maximum error before the correction: ${twoGrid.errBefore.toFixed(3)}.
Maximum error after the correction: ${twoGrid.errAfter.toFixed(3)}.`
```

## The multigrid V-cycle

Now we do a full V-cycle.  Each Jacobi step below uses $\omega = 2/3$, and
$\nu$ denotes the number of Jacobi iterations taken at each step.  The fine
grid has $m = 2^k - 1$ interior points.

1. On the fine grid, start from the straight-line initial guess, take $\nu$
   Jacobi iterations for $AU = F$, and compute the residual.
2. Going down: restrict the residual to the next coarser grid.  Starting from
   zero, take $\nu$ Jacobi iterations for the error equation $Ae = -r$ on that
   grid, and compute its residual.  Repeat until the grid has a single
   interior point.
3. Coming up: interpolate the error from each coarse grid to the next finer
   grid, subtract it from the error there, and take $\nu$ more Jacobi
   iterations.
4. On the original grid, subtract the interpolated error from $U$ and take
   $\nu$ more Jacobi iterations.

<details>
<summary>Python code from the notebook</summary>

```python
def Jacobi(U,f,alpha,beta,m,nu):
    """Perform nu Jacobi iterations on a grid with m points, with initial guess U, right hand side function f and
       Dirichlet boundary conditions with values alpha and beta.  The function returns both the approximate
       solution and the residual."""
    omega=2./3.
    h=1./(m+1)
    F=0.5*h**2*f.copy()
    F[0]-=alpha/2.; F[-1]-=beta/2.
    e=np.ones(m-1)
    G=0.5*(np.diag(e,-1)+np.diag(e,1))
    for i in range(nu):
        U=(1.-omega)*U + omega*(np.dot(G,U)-F)
    A=2./h**2*(G-np.eye(m))
    FF=f.copy(); FF[0]-=alpha/h**2; FF[-1]-=beta/h**2
    rr=FF-np.dot(A,U)
    return U,rr

k=10;
m=2**k-1
rdep=k-1  # Recursion depth; this is how many grids down we want to go
          # rdep=k-1 gives a full V-cycle
nu=3      # Number of Jacobi iterations to take at each step
U=np.linspace(alpha,beta,m)  # Initial guess
x=np.linspace(0,1,m+2); x=x[1:-1]  # grid
F=f(x)
r=[None]*(rdep+1); error=[None]*(rdep+1)
U,rr=Jacobi(U,F,alpha,beta,m,nu)  # Initial iteration on fine grid
for i in range(1,rdep+1): # Going down
    m=(m-1)//2 #  = 2**(k-i) - 1
    r[i]=coarsen(rr)             # residual restricted to next coarser grid
    error[i],rr=Jacobi(np.zeros(m),-r[i],0.,0.,m,nu)
for i in range(1,rdep): # Coming up
    m=2*m+1
    err=error[rdep-i]-interpolate(error[rdep+1-i],0,0)     # Interpolate and subtract the correction
    error[-i-1],rr=Jacobi(err,-r[rdep-i],0.,0.,m,nu)
m=2*m+1
U=U-interpolate(error[1],0,0)                   # final solution correction
U,rr=Jacobi(U,F,alpha,beta,m,nu)                #Final iterations on original grid
```

</details>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof vk = Inputs.range([5, 10], {value: 10, step: 1, label: tex`k`})
viewof vnu = Inputs.range([1, 6], {value: 3, step: 1, label: tex`\nu`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
vcycle = {
  const {alpha, beta, jacobi, coarsen, interpolate} = lib;
  let m = 2 ** vk - 1;
  const rdep = vk - 1;  // number of coarser grids
  const x = lib.grid(m), F = x.map(lib.f), u = x.map(lib.uExact);
  const U0 = lib.line(m);
  const r = new Array(rdep + 1), error = new Array(rdep + 1);
  let [U, rr] = jacobi(U0, F, alpha, beta, vnu);
  for (let i = 1; i <= rdep; i++) {  // going down
    m = (m - 1) / 2;
    r[i] = coarsen(rr);
    [error[i], rr] = jacobi(new Float64Array(m), r[i].map(v => -v), 0, 0, vnu);
  }
  for (let i = 1; i < rdep; i++) {  // coming up
    m = 2 * m + 1;
    const ec = interpolate(error[rdep + 1 - i], 0, 0);
    const err = error[rdep - i].map((v, j) => v - ec[j]);
    [error[rdep - i], rr] = jacobi(err, r[rdep - i].map(v => -v), 0, 0, vnu);
  }
  const e1 = interpolate(error[1], 0, 0);
  [U, rr] = jacobi(U.map((v, j) => v - e1[j]), F, alpha, beta, vnu);
  const Ud = lib.solveDiscrete(F, alpha, beta);
  return {
    pts: Array.from(x, (xi, i) => ({x: xi, u: u[i], U: U[i], err: U[i] - u[i]})),
    error, rdep, m: x.length,
    errInit: lib.maxAbs(U0.map((v, i) => v - u[i])),
    err: lib.maxAbs(U.map((v, i) => v - u[i])),
    errDisc: lib.maxAbs(Ud.map((v, i) => v - u[i]))
  };
}
```

```{ojs}

  width: 700, height: 420,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: null, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Exact", "After one V-cycle", "Error"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0]),
    Plot.line(vcycle.pts, {x: "x", y: "u", stroke: () => "Exact", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(vcycle.pts, {x: "x", y: "U", stroke: () => "After one V-cycle", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(vcycle.pts, {x: "x", y: "err", stroke: () => "Error", strokeWidth: 2})

})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Fine grid: m = ${vcycle.m} interior points.
Maximum error of the initial guess: ${vcycle.errInit.toFixed(3)}.
Maximum error after one V-cycle: **${vcycle.err.toPrecision(3)}**.
Maximum error of the exact solution of the discrete system ${tex`AU = F`}
(the discretization error): ${vcycle.errDisc.toPrecision(3)}.`
```

The plotted error is $U - u$, so it includes the discretization error, and no
iterative method can make it smaller than the discretization error shown
above.  For $k = 5$ the grid is too coarse to resolve the oscillations of the
exact solution near $x = 1$, and the discretization error is large.

Since we have saved the error on each grid, we can plot them to see how they
represent the accumulation of errors at different scales.  The slider goes
from the coarsest grid (one interior point) to the finest grid on which an
error is computed (the grid just below the original one).  On the coarsest
grid, the plot shows the error computed on the way down; on the other grids,
it shows the error after the correction and Jacobi iterations on the way up.
The boundary values are zero.  The vertical scale is the same for all grids.

Notice that the sign of the error alternates from one grid to the next.  The
unknown on each coarser grid is the error in the error estimate from the next
finer grid.  Because that estimate comes from a few Jacobi iterations starting
from zero, it contains little of the smooth part of the error, so the error in
it is roughly the negative of the error it is trying to approximate.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof level = Inputs.range([1, vcycle.rdep], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Grid (1 = coarsest)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const e = vcycle.error[vcycle.rdep + 1 - level];
  // Same vertical scale on every grid: at least [-5, 5] (as in the notebook),
  // enlarged if any grid's error goes beyond that.
  const ymax = Math.max(5, ...vcycle.error.slice(1).map(lib.maxAbs));
  const xs = lib.linspace(0, 1, e.length + 2);
  const pts = xs.map((x, i) => ({x, y: i === 0 || i === xs.length - 1 ? 0 : e[i - 1]}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 380,
    title: `Error on the grid with ${e.length} interior point${e.length === 1 ? "" : "s"}`,
    x: {label: "x", domain: [0, 1]},
    y: {label: null, domain: [-ymax, ymax], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "y", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(e.length <= 127 ? pts : [], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "currentColor", r: 3})
    ]
  });
}
```

## Conclusion

Now you have the basic ideas of multigrid.  Of course, for this
one-dimensional problem (where the system to be solved is tridiagonal) it does
not provide a big advantage over more naive methods.  The power of multigrid
is that it can be used in multiple dimensions, where the algebraic system is
much more challenging for other methods.  Furthermore, multigrid can be
applied to nonlinear and time-dependent problems.
